column5: YHWH's straight ways and walkers
column6: The commentary says a road is recognized by its travelers; Hosea closes by saying YHWH's ways are right, the righteous walk in them, and rebels stumble, a particularly compact formulation of the ayah's contrast.

column5: God teaches sinners the way
column6: The commentary frames the ayah as a plea for guidance to the road of God's favored people; Psalm 25:8 says the good and upright Lord therefore teaches sinners his way, pairing divine character with instruction for the errant.

column5: God's paths are covenant love and faithfulness
column6: The commentary identifies the good road by its walkers and destination; Psalm 25:10 says all the Lord's paths are steadfast love and faithfulness for those who keep his covenant, specifying what the path offers its companions.

column5: remember mercy in wrath
column6: The commentary places the bestowed favor beside those under wrath; Habakkuk asks God to revive his work and, in wrath, remember mercy, a prayer that holds judgment and favor together.

column5: Moses intercedes against divine anger
column6: The commentary notes that the same people may move from received favor to feared wrath; after the calf, Moses asks God to turn from fierce anger against Israel, making intercession a response to that transition.

column5: God relents after the intercession
column6: The commentary leaves return open after wrath; following Moses' plea in the calf episode, this verse says the Lord relented from the threatened disaster, showing the people's condition can change.

column5: anger is brief, favor lasts a lifetime
column6: The commentary juxtaposes those who receive favor and those under wrath; the psalm says God's anger lasts a moment while his favor lasts a lifetime, giving the contrast a temporal shape.

column5: Abraham blessed to become a blessing
column6: The commentary names a people by God's act of favor; God tells Abraham he will bless him and make him a blessing, so bestowed favor turns its recipient into a source of good for others.

column5: a new generation does not know YHWH
column6: The commentary says the favored generations do not pass the path automatically to their heirs; Judges says the generation after Joshua arose without knowing YHWH or his deeds, explaining how descendants can lose the inherited way.

column5: descendants warned against their fathers' path
column6: The commentary says descendants must walk as the favored did rather than inherit their standing; Psalm 78:8 urges the next generation not to be like their stubborn, faithless fathers, making faithful transmission a learned response.

column5: forgetting the giver leads to ruin
column6: The commentary says favor can be lost when its recipients change their conduct; Deuteronomy warns that forgetting YHWH and following other gods will lead to destruction, a concrete reversal from gift to judgment.

column5: return and obey after curse
column6: The commentary allows people who have strayed to return to the guided path; Deuteronomy pictures exiles returning to YHWH and obeying him with heart and soul, after the preceding blessings and curses have come upon them.

column5: repentance can turn sins into merits
column6: The commentary treats guidance and straying as states that can change; Yoma interprets repentance from love as making prior deliberate sins count as merits, extending the possibility of reversal beyond simple pardon.

column5: mercy shown on the road defines the neighbor
column6: The commentary says the way is known by the people who walk it; after the wounded traveler is passed by a priest and Levite, Jesus identifies the neighbor as the one who showed mercy and commands the hearer to do likewise.

column5: the foreigner returns to give God glory
column6: The commentary links favor received from God with joining the company of the righteous; after ten are healed, Jesus asks why only the foreigner returned to give glory to God, distinguishing gratitude and return from merely receiving a gift.

column5: Christ leaves footsteps for followers
column6: The commentary describes the requested path as the trace left by earlier walkers; Peter says Christ suffered leaving an example so others might follow in his steps, making the guide's life a traversable pattern.

column5: straight paths made crooked
column6: The commentary distinguishes the straight route from being led astray; Paul rebukes Elymas for trying to make the Lord's straight paths crooked, a concrete image of a person redirecting others from the way.

column5: leaving the straight way to follow Balaam
column6: The commentary says the path can be lost by following earlier strayers; Peter says false teachers abandoned the straight way and went astray, following Balaam's path, linking a changed route to the company one imitates.

column5: make straight paths for the feet
column6: The commentary emphasizes a road walked by actual feet and the form of walking; Hebrews commands readers to make straight paths for their feet so the lame limb may be healed rather than put out of joint.

column5: walk in good works prepared by God
column6: The commentary holds divine favor and human walking together; Ephesians says people are God's workmanship, created for good works that God prepared beforehand for them to walk in, joining gift to practiced conduct.

column5: darkness leaves a traveler unsure where he goes
column6: The commentary describes straying as a journey whose direction and destination disappear; Jesus warns that one who walks in darkness does not know where he is going, giving that lostness a precise image.

column5: claimants excluded while patriarchs feast
column6: The commentary says the path is not guaranteed by descent from blessed ancestors; Jesus pictures some seeing Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the prophets in God's kingdom while they themselves are thrown out, reversing inherited confidence.

column5: Jesus joins disciples on the road
column6: The commentary describes the path as a shared walk whose travelers can guide one another; on the Emmaus road Jesus draws near and walks with two disciples, then interprets the scriptures to them, making companionship part of how the route is understood.

column5: wrath falls on those obeying unrighteousness
column6: The commentary distinguishes wrath-struck people from active wanderers while allowing their conditions to meet; Paul says those who disobey truth and obey unrighteousness receive wrath, explicitly connecting a chosen course with judgment.

column5: walking, standing, sitting as a progression
column6: The commentary identifies a person's path by the company and actions along it; Augustine reads Psalm 1's movement from walking in wicked counsel to standing in sin's way and sitting among scoffers as increasing entrenchment, sharpening the way's moral development.
